question: Published on 6 May 20261, an investigation by newspaper Le Monde – conducted in cooperation with the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), daily De Tijd and France 2 – has revealed that a number of doctors who had been struck off or barred from the profession in France have managed to keep practising in Belgium, and vice versa.

This is despite alerts issued via the internal market information system (IMI). Alarmingly, the investigation found that France had consulted none of the over 2 000 IMI alerts analysed between 2021 and 2025, while Belgium had checked fewer than 2 %.

This state of affairs highlights major shortcomings in the alert mechanism provided for in Article 56 of Directive 2013/55/EU amending Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications. 1.

In light of the above, does the Commission intend to examine the extent to which the relevant Member State authorities consult and follow up on notifications, as well as the uniformity of compliance with the exchange-of-information obligations, in order to gauge the true effectiveness of the EU’s IMI alert mechanism?

In the interests of preventing the circumvention of national decisions and ensuring better protection for patients within the EU, is it also planning to tighten obligations regarding the systematic consultation, confirmation of receipt and traceability of alerts concerning the most serious cases of medical disciplinary action?

Anne Michel, ‘How sanctioned doctors keep practicing across the French-Belgian border’, Le Monde, Les Décodeurs, French original published 6 May 2026 (updated 8 May 2026) Available online at: https://www.lemonde.fr/en/les-decodeurs/article/2026/05/08/how-sanctioned-doctors-kept-practicing-across-thefrench-belgian-border_6753239_8.html 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Alert Mechanism set out in Directive 2005/36/EC1 concerns certain professionals (including doctors) who are prohibited or restricted from pursuing professional activities. Member States are obliged to send alerts in the cases set out in the Directive.
However, in line with the division of competencies in this area between the EU and the Member States2, it is for the Member States to decide how to follow up on those alerts.

In any case, the Commission continuously monitors compliance by Member States with their obligations to send the alerts and focuses on continuous improvements of the Internal Market Information System and facilitating its use by the national authorities.

The new guidelines concerning alerts were published in January 20263 and training sessions were provided to over 500 competent authorities in December 2025 and in March 2026. The Commission has also organised discussions with Member States’ experts to facilitate exchange of best practices concerning legal and operational frameworks to follow up on alerts.

New IT developments have also been deployed, improving the search functionality, providing more information about the reasons of alerts, and allowing the Member States to re-evaluate and improve allocation of alert-handling duties to competent authorities.

Furthermore, when developing new policy initiatives (the Skills Portability Initiative, Action 2)4, the Commission reflects on further integrating handling of alerts into possible common digital solutions and other related policy measures.
